passage_text: Researchers studied 300 adults aged 30–65 to evaluate the impact of a 12‑week aerobic exercise program on cardiovascular risk factors. Participants were randomly assigned to an exercise group (n = 150) or a control group (n = 150). Baseline measurements included age, body mass index (BMI), systolic blood pressure (SBP), and total cholesterol. After the intervention, the exercise group showed significant reductions in SBP and cholesterol compared to controls. The study also reported mean values and standard deviations for each variable, along with p‑values indicating statistical significance. The authors concluded that regular aerobic exercise can lower cardiovascular risk markers in middle‑aged adults.
stem: The variables in Table 1 are measured in different units, so their spread is best compared with the coefficient of variation (CV = SD/mean). Which variable has the largest coefficient of variation?
explanation: Correct: A) Age has CV = 8.5/48.2 = 17.6%, the largest relative spread. Why the others are wrong: B) BMI CV = 3.1/27.4 = 11.3%. C) SBP CV = 12.4/128.5 = 9.6%. D) Cholesterol CV = 25.7/210.3 = 12.2%; it has the largest absolute SD but not the largest SD relative to its mean.
trap: Choosing cholesterol because its SD (25.7 mg/dL) is the largest raw number, without scaling each SD by its own mean.

stem: Which study design would best establish a causal relationship between aerobic exercise and reduced cholesterol?

options.A: Cross‑sectional survey of exercise habits and cholesterol levels
options.B: Case‑control study comparing past exercisers to non‑exercisers
options.C: Randomized controlled trial with an exercise and a control group
options.D: Cohort study following participants over 10 years

explanation: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) with random assignment to exercise and control groups controls for confounding variables and can demonstrate causality.
trap: Students might choose the cohort study (D) because it follows participants over time, but without randomization it cannot definitively prove causation.

trap: Using the SD in place of the standard error produces a far wider interval.

stem: Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage and Table 1?

options.A: The exercise group showed significantly greater reductions in SBP and cholesterol than controls.
options.B: Participants were randomly assigned to exercise or control.
options.C: The exercise group had fewer heart attacks than the control group.
options.D: Mean baseline BMI of the study population was 27.4 kg/m².

explanation: Correct: Only risk markers (SBP, cholesterol) were measured over 12 weeks; no cardiovascular events are reported. Why the others are wrong: A) the passage states exercise group reductions in SBP and cholesterol were significant versus controls. B) the passage states random assignment to groups of 150. D) Table 1 lists BMI as 27.4 (3.1) kg/m².
trap: Assuming improved risk markers means the study showed fewer cardiovascular events.

stem: Which of the following best links this study’s findings to the broader context of cardiovascular disease prevention?

options.A: It shows that diet alone is sufficient to reduce cardiovascular risk.
options.B: It supports the view that aerobic exercise is a modifiable lifestyle factor that can improve surrogate markers of cardiovascular health.
options.C: It indicates that genetic factors are the primary determinants of cholesterol levels.
options.D: It demonstrates that medication is unnecessary for all middle‑aged adults.

explanation: Correct: B) The reductions in SBP and cholesterol support exercise as a modifiable lifestyle factor that improves surrogate markers of cardiovascular health. Why the others are wrong: A) the study tested exercise, not diet, so it says nothing about diet alone. C) the study did not examine genetic determinants of cholesterol. D) one 12-week exercise trial cannot show that medication is unnecessary for all middle-aged adults.
trap: Students may incorrectly select option D, overgeneralizing the study’s results to all adults without considering the study’s scope and limitations.
